name: Bivamelagon

lead: Bivamelagon is an experimental once-daily oral drug that activates the MC4R, a brain receptor involved in appetite and weight regulation. Fat-loss followers watch it as a possible appetite-control route to a leaner look.

It stimulates MC4R signalling in the brain's weight-regulating pathway, the chain being lower hunger, lower intake and less body fat. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in acquired hypothalamic obesity (weight gain after hypothalamic damage) was reported in the Journal of the Endocrine Society in 2025, with a long-term extension study starting afterward. No data exist in cosmetic or general fat-loss use.

paras: It has been used only in clinical trials, as a once-daily pill in people with hypothalamic obesity. There is no consumer routine.
Not approved anywhere. Safety data are limited to early trials in a small patient group, so effects in other people are unknown.

angle.text: Bivamelagon is an oral MC4R agonist that acts on the brain's appetite pathway, so hunger and intake fall and body fat follows. It has been studied in phase 2 for weight gain after hypothalamic damage.

lead: Bivamelagon (also LB54640 and LR-19021) is an investigational oral drug that activates the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), a brain pathway involved in appetite and energy balance. It is being developed for hypothalamic obesity, weight gain that follows damage to the hypothalamus, and its link to appearance runs through body weight and body fat: a drug that lowers hunger and weight could change body composition and how lean a person looks.[1][2][3]

Wikipedia describes it as a small-molecule MC4 receptor agonist under development by LG Chem Life Sciences, and notes that unlike the older MC4R agonist setmelanotide, which is given by injection, it can be taken by mouth.[4][5] Setmelanotide (Imcivree) was approved in the US in November 2020 and in the EU in July 2021 for obesity caused by certain rare genetic conditions.[5]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in acquired hypothalamic obesity was reported in the Journal of the Endocrine Society in 2025.[1] A registered phase 2 study (n=28) is complete and a long-term extension study (n=25) began enrolling by invitation in November 2025.[2][3] Bivamelagon is not an approved drug.

paras: Wikipedia describes hypothalamic obesity as a rare condition that can be congenital or acquired. Congenital forms include Prader-Willi syndrome and mutations in genes such as LEP, LEPR, POMC, MC4R and CART, while acquired forms follow hypothalamic injury from trauma, therapeutic radiation or brain surgery, with craniopharyngioma and its treatments especially named. It lists bariatric surgery and MC4R agonists such as setmelanotide among treatments.[6]

Bivamelagon is a small-molecule agonist of the melanocortin-4 receptor.[4] Setmelanotide, which acts at the same receptor, activates MC4 receptors in hypothalamic areas that regulate appetite, increases resting energy expenditure and, unlike some other MC4R agonists, has not been found to raise heart rate or blood pressure, according to Wikipedia.[5] A 2026 review in Frontiers in Endocrinology describes the melanocortin system, particularly MC4R, as a validated obesity target involved in food intake, weight control and energy expenditure, and notes that many MC4R-selective agonists were abandoned in the clinic because of insufficient potency, poor selectivity or side effects.[7]

A 2026 review in Acta Pharmaceutica Sinica B describes renewed efforts to develop MC4R modulators, citing structural work and Gq/11 signalling in paraventricular nucleus neurons as central to appetite suppression, and calls for next-generation therapies including combinations with GLP-1 mimetics.[7]

Wikipedia reports that in two one-year studies of 10 and 11 participants (POMC or PCSK1 deficiency, and LEPR deficiency) most lost more than 10 percent of initial body weight on setmelanotide, and some reported feeling less hungry.[5] Common setmelanotide side effects listed there include injection-site reactions, skin hyperpigmentation, headache and gastrointestinal problems, with spontaneous penile erections and sexual adverse reactions also reported, and depression and suicidal ideation noted in some people.[5] Wikipedia lists bivamelagon among other MC4 agonists without describing its adverse effects.[4]

Wikipedia cites a 2022 first-in-human safety and pharmacodynamics study in the journal Obesity and notes that phase 2 trials were complete as of February 2026, with Rhythm Pharmaceuticals named in connection with the trials.[4] Wikipedia credits Rhythm with development of setmelanotide, which was invented at Ipsen.[5] The registry listing NCT06046443 began in July 2024 and is complete, and NCT07156578 is a long-term follow-up study started in November 2025.[2][3]

The phase 2 trial in acquired hypothalamic obesity tested once-daily oral bivamelagon against placebo in a double-blind, multicenter design and was reported as a 2025 conference abstract in the Journal of the Endocrine Society.[1] The registry listing NCT06046443 is complete (28 participants, started July 2024), and NCT07156578 is a long-term follow-up (25 participants, started November 2025).[2][3] Quantitative results were not available in the sources loaded for this article. No studies were found in healthy people seeking cosmetic fat loss.

timeline.event: Setmelanotide, the injectable MC4R agonist, is approved in the US.[5]
Setmelanotide is approved in the EU.[5]
First-in-human safety and pharmacodynamics study of bivamelagon is published in Obesity.[4]
Phase 2 study in hypothalamic obesity begins.[2]
Phase 2 results presented; long-term study starts.[1][3]
